findings.title: Sleep regularity

bands.label: below 71.6
bands.headline: Your sleep is less regular than the least-regular fifth of a large UK cohort, the group that had the highest mortality risk. In that study sleep regularity predicted mortality more strongly than sleep duration. Later studies found that sleeping enough hours didn't cancel out the higher risk of heart disease and depression that came with irregular sleep.
bands.detail: In 60,977 UK Biobank participants (mean age 63) followed for about 6 years, the median Sleep Regularity Index was 81.0 (middle half 73.8 to 86.3). Compared with the least-regular fifth (below 71.6), the more regular groups had a 20-48% lower risk of all-cause mortality. In 61 university students, the least regular sleepers had their melatonin rhythm about 2.5 hours later than the most regular ones (around midnight versus 21:32) and did worse academically, even though they slept as many hours. In a later analysis of 72,269 UK Biobank adults followed for 8 years, people below 71.6 had a 26% higher risk of heart attack, stroke or heart failure than the most regular sleepers (above 87.3), and sleeping the recommended hours didn't offset it (hazard ratio 1.19, 1.06-1.35). In 79,666 adults followed for 7.5 years, the least regular quarter had a higher risk of new depression and anxiety; even those who slept the recommended hours had a 48% higher risk of depression (hazard ratio 1.48, 1.18-1.86) than regular sleepers who did. In 88,094 adults, an index at the 5th percentile went with a 53% higher risk of dementia than the median (hazard ratio 1.53, 1.24-1.89).

bands.headline: Your sleep regularity is below the median of a large UK cohort but above its least-regular fifth, the group with the highest mortality risk.
bands.detail: In UK Biobank the median Sleep Regularity Index was 81.0 (middle half 73.8 to 86.3); the least-regular fifth scored below 71.6. In a heart study of 72,269 UK Biobank adults, people between 71.6 and 87.3 had a slightly higher risk of heart attack, stroke or heart failure than the most regular sleepers (8%), but not if they also slept the recommended hours (hazard ratio 1.07, 0.96-1.18). Below 71.6, enough sleep didn't offset the risk.

bands.label: 81 and above
bands.headline: Your sleep is at least as regular as the median of a large UK cohort, where more regular sleep was linked to lower mortality.
bands.detail: In UK Biobank the median Sleep Regularity Index was 81.0 (middle half 73.8 to 86.3). In a heart study of 72,269 UK Biobank adults, the most regular group scored above 87.3; between 71.6 and 87.3 the risk of heart attack, stroke or heart failure was slightly higher (8%), but not for people who also slept the recommended hours.

findings.background: The Sleep Regularity Index is the chance of being in the same state, asleep or awake, at two moments 24 hours apart: 100 means identical days, 0 means random. Your bedtime varies by about {bedtime_sd_h:.1f} hours (standard deviation) and your wake time by about {wake_sd_h:.1f} hours. Your typical time asleep is {asleep_h:.1f} h.
findings.caveat: The studies measured sleep with research accelerometers; this score uses your tracker's sleep stages and only pairs of consecutive days that both have a recorded night. The UK Biobank cohort was much older than most readers. Treat the comparison as indicative. Studies compute the index differently: on the same UK Biobank data, the depression study's cut-offs (51 and 71) were much lower than the heart study's (71.6 and 87.3), and the dementia study's median was 60, so treat the numbers as rough guides.

findings.title: Late sleep timing

bands.label: less than 1 h after {usual_bedtime_clock}
bands.headline: Your typical sleep onset ({bedtime_clock}) is close to the {usual_bedtime_clock} bedtime your schedule asks of you.

bands.label: 1-2 h after {usual_bedtime_clock}
bands.headline: Your typical sleep onset ({bedtime_clock}) is 1-2 hours after the {usual_bedtime_clock} bedtime your schedule asks of you: late, but less than the two hours that characterise delayed sleep-wake phase disorder.
bands.detail: A late body clock is also common in ADHD: a review found delayed sleep phase in 73-78% of children and adults with ADHD. Late sleep on its own doesn't point to ADHD, and a sleep tracker can't tell; but if problems with attention, restlessness or impulsivity have played a role since childhood, mention them to your doctor alongside your sleep.

bands.label: 2 h or more after {usual_bedtime_clock}
bands.headline: You typically fall asleep at {bedtime_clock} and wake at {wake_clock}: {bedtime_delay_h:.1f} hours after the {usual_bedtime_clock} bedtime your schedule asks of you. Sleep timing delayed by more than two hours is what characterises delayed sleep-wake phase disorder (DSWPD). Only a clinician can diagnose it.
bands.detail: The AASM guideline describes DSWPD as habitual sleep timing that is delayed, usually by more than two hours, relative to conventional or socially acceptable times, with difficulty falling asleep and waking at the required times; when people with DSWPD can follow their own schedule, sleep quality and quantity are typically normal. For adults it suggests strategically timed melatonin (a weak recommendation). It found insufficient evidence to recommend morning light therapy on its own for adults; for children and adolescents it suggests light after waking combined with behavioural treatment. Diagnosed DSWPD usually starts in adolescence or young adulthood, and its prevalence in adolescents and young adults is estimated at 1-16%. A late body clock is also common in ADHD: a review found delayed sleep phase in 73-78% of children and adults with ADHD. Late sleep on its own doesn't point to ADHD, and a sleep tracker can't tell; but if problems with attention, restlessness or impulsivity have played a role since childhood, mention them to your doctor alongside your sleep.

findings.background: Late timing is measured from the bedtime in your settings ({usual_bedtime_clock}). Your typical mid-point of sleep is {midsleep_clock}.
findings.caveat: Late timing alone isn't a disorder. The diagnosis also depends on whether it causes problems with the times you need to keep, and on how you sleep on a free schedule; a sleep diary like the one in this report is part of the assessment.

findings.title: Evening naps

bands.label: fewer than 1 a month
bands.headline: Hardly any evening naps: {evening_naps:.0f} in {nights:.0f} nights.

bands.label: up to 2 a month
bands.headline: You took {evening_naps:.0f} evening naps in {nights:.0f} nights, about once or twice a month. Evening naps can reduce sleep pressure and delay falling asleep at night.

bands.label: more than 2 a month
bands.headline: You often nap in the evening: {evening_naps_per_week:.1f} times a week. In an experiment, an early-evening nap made people take longer to fall asleep that night; in your own data you fell asleep {nap_bedtime_delay_min} minutes later on nights after an evening nap.
bands.detail: Your median sleep onset was {bedtime_after_evening_nap_clock} after an evening nap and {bedtime_without_evening_nap_clock} otherwise. In Werth et al., healthy young men who took an early-evening nap had a longer sleep latency and less deep-sleep (slow-wave) activity the following night than in a baseline night, consistent with reduced sleep pressure. A review of sleep-hygiene evidence notes that evening naps in particular 'may be problematic if they dissipate homeostatic drive', while finding the evidence on daytime naps overall inconclusive.

findings.caveat: Your own comparison is observational: nights after a nap may differ in other ways too (for example a short night before). The bands are this report's own; the studies didn't define how often is too often.

findings.title: Normal oxygen does not rule out a breathing-related cause of tiredness
findings.headline: Some people are very sleepy during the day because of many very short arousals caused by extra breathing effort, with only a limited reduction in breathing volume, a pattern a wrist tracker cannot see.
findings.detail: Guilleminault et al. described 15 patients with excessive daytime sleepiness whose sleep was fragmented by brief EEG arousals. Each arousal followed one to three breaths of flow limitation with an abrupt but limited reduction in tidal volume, driven by increased respiratory effort (mean peak oesophageal pressure -33 cm H2O). Treatment with nasal CPAP reduced the arousal index from 31 to 8 per hour and their sleepiness resolved (time to fall asleep in a daytime nap test from 5.1 to 13.5 minutes). Measuring this needs a sleep study with breathing-effort sensors and EEG.
findings.caveat: Shown because you didn't say you're rarely tired. It isn't based on your data, which can't detect this either way.

findings.title: Social jetlag

bands.label: under 1 h
bands.headline: Your sleep timing hardly shifts at the weekend.

bands.label: 1-2 h
bands.headline: Your sleep shifts {social_jetlag_h:.1f} hours later on weekend nights: 'social jetlag', a mismatch between your body clock and your schedule that has been linked to higher BMI independently of sleep duration.

bands.label: 2 h or more
bands.headline: Your sleep shifts {social_jetlag_h:.1f} hours later on weekend nights: a large 'social jetlag', a mismatch between your body clock and your schedule that has been linked to higher BMI independently of sleep duration.

findings.background: Across the week your mid-sleep moves by {weekly_drift_h:.1f} hours between the earliest and the latest weekday. Social jetlag was described as the discrepancy between work and free days, between social and biological time; its links with wellbeing and stimulant use were strongest in people up to 25 years old.
findings.caveat: Free nights are the evenings before the days off in your settings. The bands are this report's own; the studies don't define a cut-off.

bands.label: under 25%

bands.label: 50% or more

findings.background: On the other side, {pct_nights_over_9h:.0f}% of your nights are over 9 hours. The consensus statement says more than 9 hours may be appropriate for young adults, people recovering from sleep debt and people with illnesses; for others it is uncertain whether it carries a health risk.
findings.caveat: The consensus statement doesn't say how many short nights are too many; these bands are this report's own.

findings.title: Nap length

bands.label: under 30 min
bands.headline: Your naps are short. In a large meta-analysis, naps under 60 minutes were not linked to higher cardiovascular risk.

bands.label: 30-59 min
bands.headline: Your naps are moderate in length. In a large meta-analysis, cardiovascular risk was lowest around 30 minutes of napping a day and rose from about 45 minutes.

bands.label: 60 min or more
bands.headline: Your typical nap is {nap_min:.0f} minutes. In a meta-analysis of 11 cohorts (151,588 people), daily naps of 60 minutes or more were associated with a higher risk of cardiovascular disease (rate ratio 1.82) and of death from any cause (1.27); naps under 60 minutes were not.
bands.detail: The risk curve for cardiovascular disease was J-shaped: lowest around 30 minutes a day, rising slightly to about 45 minutes and steeply after that. In the National Sleep Foundation panel, naps over 100 minutes were judged a sign of poor sleep quality in adults.

bands.label: 20 min or less
bands.headline: Your naps are short. For teenagers, an expert panel judged naps of 20 minutes or less a sign of good sleep quality.

bands.label: 21-120 min
bands.headline: Your typical nap is {nap_min:.0f} minutes: longer than the 20 minutes an expert panel judged good for teenagers, but not over the 120 minutes it judged poor.

bands.label: over 120 min
bands.headline: Your typical nap is {nap_min:.0f} minutes. For teenagers, an expert panel judged naps over 120 minutes a sign of poor sleep quality.

findings.caveat: These are associations in observational studies; long naps may be a sign of an underlying problem rather than its cause. Your naps were counted on {naps} occasions.

findings.title: Oxygen dips (ODI)

bands.label: under 5
bands.headline: Your oxygen dips are well under 5 per hour on a typical night (highest night {max_odi3:.1f}). In a validation study, an index above 5 was the best cut-off for detecting sleep apnea, so this gives no sign of the kind of sleep apnea that repeatedly lowers oxygen.
bands.detail: In 475 surgical patients tested with home sleep studies and high-resolution oximetry at the same time, an oxygen desaturation index above 5, 15 and 30 per hour best matched an apnea-hypopnea index above 5, 15 and 30 (accuracy 86%, 86% and 94%). The AASM uses 5, 15 and 30 events per hour as its sleep-apnea severity thresholds.

bands.headline: Your oxygen dips are between 5 and 15 per hour, the range that matched mild sleep apnea in a validation study. Worth discussing with a doctor.
Your oxygen dips are between 15 and 30 per hour, the range that matched moderate sleep apnea in a validation study. Please discuss this with a doctor.

bands.label: 30 or more
bands.headline: Your oxygen dips are 30 or more per hour, the range that matched severe sleep apnea in a validation study. Please discuss this with a doctor soon.

bands.label: adult cut-offs
bands.headline: Your oxygen dips are {odi3:.1f} per hour. The usual cut-offs (5, 15 and 30 per hour) come from adult guidelines and a study of adults around 60 years old; they don't apply to teenagers. Ask a doctor if you snore or are often tired.

findings.caveat: Fitbit reports SpO2 as a 5-minute moving average, which flattens short dips, so this count runs lower than a clinical oximeter's and can miss mild apnea. This report counts dips of 3 or more points. The AASM strongly recommends that sleep apnea be diagnosed only with a sleep study or home sleep apnea test, not with questionnaires or prediction tools.

bands.label: over 9 h

findings.background: Your time asleep varies from night to night (standard deviation {asleep_sd_h:.1f} hours). The AASM/SRS adult consensus covers ages 18 to 60; the National Sleep Foundation's ranges cover each age group.
findings.caveat: Wrist trackers tend to count quiet wakefulness as sleep, so real sleep time may be somewhat lower.

findings.title: Heart-rate surges during sleep
findings.valueLabel: Surges of 10+ bpm per hour asleep
findings.headline: Your heart rate surged by 10 or more beats per minute about {surges_per_hour:.1f} times per hour of sleep, {surges_without_awakening:.1f} of them without an awakening detected by Fitbit. Arousals from sleep reliably come with a heart-rate rise, but there's no normal range for this count from a wrist tracker.
findings.detail: In healthy adults every type of arousal came with a speeding up of the heart followed by a slowing, and the rise began before the brain arousal itself. In 28 healthy young adults the average rise per arousal ranged from 1.9 to 18.3 bpm between people, and each person's response was very consistent from night to night. In two large community cohorts, a large pulse-rate rise after breathing events during sleep predicted cardiovascular disease and death. (This report's note: repeated breathing events would show up as many surges per hour, often in a regular rhythm.)
findings.caveat: Use this to compare your own nights. Because individual heart-rate responses vary so much, a low count doesn't prove there are few arousals.

findings.title: What a wrist tracker can and can't measure
findings.headline: Fitbit trackers detect sleep well but miss much of the time spent awake, and their sleep stages are only moderately accurate, so efficiency and stage numbers in this report are estimates.
findings.detail: Against polysomnography, seven consumer trackers detected at least 93% of sleep but only 18-54% of wake; their sleep-stage results were inconsistent, though a Fitbit was the best performer overall and for light and REM sleep. In a Fitbit Charge 2 study, deep sleep was correctly identified only 49% of the time and underestimated by 24 minutes, while light sleep was overestimated by 34 minutes. A meta-analysis of Fitbit models with sleep stages found 95-96% sensitivity but 58-69% specificity for detecting sleep, and concluded they are not a substitute for a sleep study. For oxygen, a Fitbit Charge 4 agreed poorly with a medical oximeter in people with COPD and overestimated saturation, while resting heart rate and breathing rate agreed well.
findings.caveat: None of these studies tested the Charge 6 itself.

findings.title: Apnea-like heart-rate cycles
findings.valueLabel: Heart-rate cycles per hour in bed

bands.label: under 11
bands.headline: On a typical night your heart rate showed {cvhr_median:.1f} apnea-like cycles per hour in bed, below the 11 per hour that best identified moderate-to-severe sleep apnea in a study with a wrist-worn watch. The method isn't validated on Fitbit heart rate, and in your data it also finds {cvhr_awake_rate:.1f} cycles per hour while you're awake, so treat this as a rough hint, not reassurance.
bands.detail: At the start of an apnea the heart slows progressively, and it speeds up abruptly when breathing resumes, so repeated apneas make heart rate cycle. In 862 patients, the heart-rate cycle count from an all-night ECG correlated with the apnea-hypopnea index (r = 0.84), and 15 or more per hour identified moderate-to-severe apnea with 83% sensitivity and 88% specificity. With a wrist-worn watch in 41 patients it correlated at r = 0.81; 11 or more per hour identified moderate-to-severe apnea with 82% sensitivity and 89% specificity. People with moderate-to-severe apnea averaged 19.6 per hour, those without 6.4.

bands.headline: On a typical night your heart rate showed {cvhr_median:.1f} apnea-like cycles per hour in bed: between the cut-off validated with a wrist-worn watch (11) and the one validated with ECG (15). The method isn't validated on Fitbit heart rate (it also finds {cvhr_awake_rate:.1f} per hour while you're awake), so this is a hint worth mentioning to a doctor, not a finding.

bands.label: 15 or more

The method isn't validated on Fitbit heart rate, but this is worth discussing with a doctor.

bands.label: adult studies
bands.headline: Your heart rate showed {cvhr_median:.1f} apnea-like cycles per hour in bed. The cut-offs for this method come from studies in adults, so they don't apply to teenagers.

findings.background: By sleep stage your rate was {cvhr_deep_rate:.1f} per hour in deep sleep, {cvhr_nrem_rate:.1f} in light and deep sleep together, {cvhr_rem_rate:.1f} in REM sleep and {cvhr_awake_rate:.1f} while awake. Apnea doesn't happen while you're awake, so cycles detected then are a measure of how many detections are noise. {cvhr_nights_over_11} of {cvhr_nights} nights reached 11 per hour.
findings.caveat: Not validated on Fitbit data: the studies used beat-to-beat intervals from an ECG or the watch's pulse wave, while Fitbit gives a heart rate about every 2 seconds. Periodic leg movements can mimic the pattern, the count varies a lot from night to night (a 66% coefficient of variation over a week of ECG recordings), and the watch cut-off came from 41 people. A screening hint, not a measure of apnea.

findings.background: Reference values come from 8.2 million Fitbit users: RMSSD measured in 5-minute windows and summarised per hour, for each year of age. HRV is highest in the early morning and falls with age; for RMSSD there was no significant difference between men and women, so the report uses the average of both. Your deep-sleep HRV was {hrv_deep_median:.1f} ms.
findings.caveat: The reference values are for the 06:00-07:00 clock hour, near the daily peak of HRV, while Fitbit's nightly HRV covers your whole sleep, so the comparison is approximate. The values are from the study's preprint supplement.

findings.background: In that study a person's daily resting heart rate typically varied by about 3 bpm (standard deviation), and resting heart rate was lowest in people who slept 7 to 7.5 hours a night. Age, sex, BMI and sleep together explained no more than 10% of the differences between people.
findings.caveat: Resting heart rate is your device's own daily estimate.

findings.title: Nights that stood out

bands.label: none
bands.headline: No night stood out: on no night did two or more of heart rate, HRV, breathing rate and skin temperature clearly move away from your recent normal.

One night stood out, with heart rate {off_hr_delta:+.0f} bpm and HRV {off_hrv_delta:+.0f} ms compared with your normal (median). If breathing rate or skin temperature also rose that night, that's the pattern typical of illness; heart rate up and HRV down on their own is the pattern seen after drinking alcohol.
bands.detail: Illness tends to raise breathing rate and heart rate and to lower HRV, and in 2,745 people with COVID-19 breathing rate showed the largest change and took longest to recover. A rise of 3 or more breaths per minute was seen in 36% of people with symptoms but on only 4% of healthy nights. Resting heart rate rose a median 7 bpm before COVID-19 symptoms, and finger skin temperature rose by about 0.6 °C around symptoms. After alcohol, measured in 4,098 people over the first hours of sleep, heart rate rose by 1.4, 4.0 and 8.7 bpm and RMSSD fell by 2.0, 5.7 and 12.9 ms after low, moderate and high amounts, with stronger effects in younger people.

bands.label: 2 or more

In {off_with_breathing_or_temp_up} of them breathing rate or skin temperature also rose, the signals that typically rise with illness. Heart rate up and HRV down on their own is the pattern seen after drinking alcohol.

findings.background: Open the off nights from the HRV chart or the nights table to see each signal against your normal.
findings.caveat: The thresholds are this report's own: a night counts as off when at least two signals are more than 2 robust standard deviations away from your previous 28 nights, in the direction illness or alcohol push them. The studies used other methods, and late heavy meals, stress or hard exercise can have similar effects.

findings.title: Anxiety, sleep and heart-rate variability
findings.headline: People with an anxiety disorder have somewhat lower heart-rate variability on average than people without one, and poor sleep and anxiety tend to feed each other. The differences are small, and your HRV can't tell whether you have anxiety.
findings.detail: A meta-analysis of 36 studies (2,086 people with an anxiety disorder, 2,294 without) found lower high-frequency HRV in anxiety disorders, a small effect (Hedges' g -0.29), seen in panic disorder, PTSD, generalised anxiety and social anxiety but not obsessive-compulsive disorder. Time-domain measures, mostly RMSSD, were also lower (g -0.45) once one large outlying study was excluded; with it the difference wasn't significant. A systematic review of 9 mostly longitudinal studies concluded that the best available evidence suggests insomnia is related to anxiety and depression in both directions, while noting that definitive conclusions can't be made for most sleep problems.
findings.caveat: These are average differences between people diagnosed with an anxiety disorder and healthy people, measured with clinical ECG, not wrist trackers. Many things affect HRV, including age and alcohol (see the heart findings in this report). If you often feel anxious, worried or low, or sleep problems come with low mood, talk to your GP.

findings.title: Trouble sleeping and later depression
findings.valueLabel: Nights taking over 30 min to fall asleep
findings.headline: In people who weren't depressed, insomnia roughly doubled the risk of developing depression later. In your data it took more than 30 minutes to fall asleep on {pct_latency_over_30:.0f}% of nights; whether that is insomnia depends on how you experience your sleep, which a tracker can't measure.
findings.detail: A meta-analysis of 21 longitudinal studies found an odds ratio of 2.60 (1.98-3.42) for insomnia predicting depression, and 2.10 (1.86-2.38) once outlying studies were removed. The studies didn't always account for other factors.
findings.caveat: Insomnia is diagnosed from what you report (difficulty falling or staying asleep, with daytime effects), not from tracker data. If you often feel anxious, worried or low, or sleep problems come with low mood, talk to your GP.

findings.title: Late sleep timing and depression

bands.label: before 04:00
bands.headline: In a genetic study of nearly 840,000 adults, a tendency toward earlier sleep timing was linked to a lower risk of major depression: 23% lower per hour earlier mid-point of sleep. Your mid-point of sleep is {midsleep_clock}.

bands.label: 04:00 or later
bands.headline: In a genetic study of nearly 840,000 adults, a tendency toward earlier sleep timing was linked to a lower risk of major depression: 23% lower per hour earlier mid-point of sleep. Your mid-point of sleep ({midsleep_clock}) is much later than that study's average of 03:00, and its authors say the effect may not apply to such extremes, such as delayed sleep phase.

findings.detail: The study used Mendelian randomisation: genetic variants that make people prefer mornings, scaled to an accelerometer-measured mid-point of sleep (average 03:00, standard deviation 0.91 h, in 85,502 people), compared across 170,756 people with major depression and 329,443 without. The odds ratio was 0.77 (0.63-0.94) per hour earlier. Because genes act over a lifetime, the authors note the result may not reflect what a shorter-term change in sleep timing would do. In a meta-analysis of 36 questionnaire studies (15,734 people), an evening preference went with somewhat more depressive symptoms (a small association, Fisher's z -0.20).
findings.caveat: These are population-level associations, mostly in people of European ancestry; they don't say anything about your own mood. If you often feel low or have lost interest in things, talk to your GP.

findings.title: Falling asleep before 02:00
findings.valueLabel: Nights before a workday you fell asleep between 20:00 and 02:00

bands.label: below 93.5%
bands.headline: On {pct_workdays_onset_20_02:.0f}% of nights before a workday you fell asleep between 20:00 and 02:00. In 6,785 Fitbit users the median was 93.5%, and people below it had 70% higher odds of being diagnosed with major depression.

bands.label: 93.5% or more
bands.headline: On {pct_workdays_onset_20_02:.0f}% of nights before a workday you fell asleep between 20:00 and 02:00: at or above the median of 6,785 Fitbit users, among whom people below the median had higher odds of depression.

findings.detail: The study linked 4.5 years (median) of Fitbit data from 6,785 participants of the All of Us Research Program to their health records (median age 50, 71% women). It counted the share of weekdays with sleep onset in 'traditional' hours, 20:00 to 02:00 (median 93.5%). Compared with people above the median, those below it had an odds ratio of 1.70 (1.42-2.03) for major depressive disorder, and higher odds of insomnia (1.74) and high blood pressure (1.60). A UK Biobank study of 73,888 middle-aged and older adults, with sleep timed by a research accelerometer, found more depression and anxiety in people who slept late whatever their own preference: evening types who slept early had a lower risk of depression than evening types who slept late. Its authors suggest falling asleep before 01:00, a cut-off they present as a hypothesis. You fell asleep after 01:00 on {pct_onset_after_01:.0f}% of all your nights.
findings.background: Your typical sleep onset is {bedtime_clock}. Nights before a workday are the evenings before days that aren't days off in your settings.
findings.caveat: Observational: low mood can push sleep later as well as the other way round, and people who sleep late may differ in other ways. Most participants in both studies were middle-aged or older; whether the same holds for young adults isn't known. The Fitbit study counted weekdays; this report counts evenings before the days that aren't off in your settings. If you often feel low or have lost interest in things, talk to your GP.

findings.title: Irregular sleep and mood

bands.label: up to 1 h 44 min
bands.headline: Your wake-up time varies about as much as, or less than, it did for junior doctors before their internship started, in a Fitbit study where more variable sleep went with more depressive symptoms and lower next-day mood.

bands.label: over 1 h 44 min
bands.headline: Your wake-up time varies more from night to night ({wake_sd_h:.1f} h standard deviation) than it did for junior doctors before their internship started (1 h 44 min), in a Fitbit study where more variable wake-up times and sleep durations went with more depressive symptoms and lower next-day mood.

findings.detail: In 2,115 interns wearing a Fitbit Charge 2, the night-to-night standard deviation of sleep time was associated with depressive symptoms even with average sleep time taken into account, and variability in sleep time and wake-up time was associated with lower mood the next day. Before the internship the typical spreads were 1 h 15 min for sleep time, 1 h 39 min for bedtime and 1 h 44 min for wake-up time. The amount of variation in depressive symptoms explained by sleep variability was small, and the authors note the design precludes conclusions about causality.
findings.background: Your spreads: {asleep_sd_h:.1f} h for time asleep, {bedtime_sd_h:.1f} h for bedtime and {wake_sd_h:.1f} h for wake-up time (standard deviations).
findings.caveat: The interns' reference values come from only about 17 days of recording before a demanding job; the study's sleep time included naps, while this report's spread of time asleep counts main sleeps only. The bands are this report's own. If you often feel low or have lost interest in things, talk to your GP.

findings.title: Night-to-night spread of sleep length
findings.valueLabel: Night-to-night spread of time asleep (standard deviation)

bands.label: under 1 h
bands.headline: How long you sleep varies by {asleep_sd_h:.1f} h from night to night (standard deviation). In 6,785 Fitbit users followed for years, a larger spread went with higher odds of depression, anxiety and bipolar disorder, even with average sleep length taken into account.

bands.label: 1 h or more
bands.headline: How long you sleep varies by {asleep_sd_h:.1f} h from night to night (standard deviation). In 6,785 Fitbit users followed for years, each extra hour of spread went with 75% higher odds of a depression diagnosis, and also with anxiety and bipolar disorder, even with average sleep length taken into account.

findings.detail: The study linked 4.5 years (median) of Fitbit data from 6,785 participants of the All of Us Research Program to their health records (median age 50, 71% women). The spread was the standard deviation of daily main-sleep duration in hours, the same measure as here. Per hour of spread, the odds ratios were 1.75 (1.52-2.01) for major depressive disorder, 1.55 (1.35-1.78) for anxiety disorder and 2.27 (1.65-3.11) for bipolar disorder, adjusted for age, sex, daily steps and length of health record; the spread was also linked to high blood pressure, obesity and sleep apnea. 23 of 24 of these links held after adjusting for average sleep duration. In a stricter analysis that followed people over time, the 75th compared with the 25th percentile of spread went with a hazard ratio of 1.17 (0.96-1.42) for new depression, which wasn't statistically clear.
findings.background: Your typical time asleep is {asleep_h:.1f} h. The spread counts your main sleep of every recorded night; naps aren't included.
findings.caveat: Observational: irregular sleep can follow from low mood as well as lead to it. The study reported odds per hour of spread, not cut-offs; the bands are this report's own. Participants were healthier and wealthier than average, and most were older than 35. If you often feel low or have lost interest in things, talk to your GP.

findings.title: Short nights and how alert you are

bands.label: under 10%
bands.headline: Short nights (under 6 hours asleep) are rare for you. In a laboratory study, people restricted to 6 hours or less for two weeks performed as badly as after up to two nights without sleep.

{pct_nights_under_6h:.0f}% of your nights are under 6 hours asleep. In a laboratory study, restricting sleep to 6 hours or less for two weeks built up deficits in attention and thinking equivalent to up to two nights without sleep, while people's own sleepiness ratings suggested they were largely unaware of it.

bands.label: 30% or more
bands.headline: {pct_nights_under_6h:.0f}% of your nights are under 6 hours asleep. In a laboratory study, restricting sleep to 6 hours or less for two weeks built up deficits in attention and thinking equivalent to up to two nights without sleep, while people's own sleepiness ratings suggested they were largely unaware of it.

findings.detail: 48 healthy adults aged 21-38 were randomised to 4, 6 or 8 hours in bed for 14 consecutive days, or 3 nights without sleep. The 4 and 6 hour groups developed cumulative, dose-dependent deficits on all tasks. Sleepiness ratings rose at first and then only a little further, and didn't distinguish 6 from 4 hours.
findings.background: Your short nights came at most {max_short_run:.0f} in a row, while the deficits in the study built up over 14 consecutive nights.
findings.caveat: The study restricted time in bed; this report counts time asleep, which is shorter than time in bed. The bands are this report's own.

findings.title: Irregular sleep and heart disease
findings.valueLabel: Typical spread of sleep-onset time within a week

bands.label: 30 min or less
bands.headline: Within a week, the time you fall asleep typically varies by {onset_sd7_min:.0f} minutes (standard deviation): as regular as the group with the lowest risk of cardiovascular events in a large cohort study.
bands.detail: In 1,992 adults without heart disease who wore a research actigraph for 7 days, followed for a median of 4.9 years, the risk of cardiovascular events (heart attack, stroke, cardiac death and related events) rose with the 7-day spread of sleep-onset time: compared with 30 minutes or less, the adjusted hazard ratio was 1.16 for 31-60 minutes, 1.52 for 61-90 minutes and 2.11 for more than 90 minutes; only the last was statistically significant. The association persisted after adjusting for average sleep duration.

findings.background: Your time asleep typically varies by {asleep_sd7_min:.0f} minutes within a week. In the same study, a spread of sleep duration over 120 minutes went with a hazard ratio of 2.14 (91-120 minutes: 1.59, not statistically significant).
findings.caveat: Participants were 45 to 84 years old when the cohort started, so the study can't say what this means for younger people. It's observational: the authors note reverse causation and unmeasured confounding can't be excluded. The study used 7 days of research actigraphy; this report uses the median of all your 7-night windows from your tracker.

findings.title: Short sleep and catching a cold

bands.label: none
bands.headline: In none of your weeks did your sleep average under 6 hours, the level at which volunteers exposed to a cold virus got sick about four times as often as those sleeping more than 7 hours. {pct_weeks_6_to_7h:.0f}% of your weeks averaged 6 to 7 hours, where the risk wasn't clearly higher.
bands.detail: 164 healthy adults aged 18 to 55 wore a wrist actigraph for 7 nights, then were quarantined, given nasal drops with a common cold virus and followed for 5 days. A clinical cold meant infection plus objective signs of illness. Compared with sleeping more than 7 hours, the odds of a cold were 4.50 times higher with under 5 hours and 4.24 times higher with 5 to 6 hours; 6 to 7 hours carried no clearly higher risk (1.66, not significant). This held independent of prior antibody levels, demographics, season, BMI, psychological factors and health practices; how fragmented sleep was didn't matter.

bands.label: 1% or more
bands.headline: In {pct_weeks_under_6h:.0f}% of your weeks your sleep averaged under 6 hours. Volunteers exposed to a cold virus after a week like that got sick about four times as often as those sleeping more than 7 hours.
bands.detail: 164 healthy adults aged 18 to 55 wore a wrist actigraph for 7 nights, then were quarantined, given nasal drops with a common cold virus and followed for 5 days. A clinical cold meant infection plus objective signs of illness. Compared with sleeping more than 7 hours, the odds of a cold were 4.50 times higher with under 5 hours and 4.24 times higher with 5 to 6 hours; 6 to 7 hours carried no clearly higher risk (1.66, not significant). This held independent of prior antibody levels, demographics, season, BMI, psychological factors and health practices; how fragmented sleep was didn't matter.

findings.caveat: A small study with wide confidence intervals. The authors note it doesn't provide direct evidence of causality, although sleep was measured before the virus, which rules out reverse causation.

findings.title: What an Apple Watch can and can't measure here
findings.headline: An Apple Watch records sleep stages, breathing rate, wrist temperature and resting heart rate well enough for most of this report. It measures blood oxygen only now and then and heart rate every few minutes during sleep, so oxygen dips, heart-rate surges and apnea-like heart-rate cycles can't be counted, and its HRV (SDNN) can't be compared with the RMSSD reference values.
findings.detail: The watch decides when it measures blood oxygen and heart rate; apps can't change that. Apple's own sleep apnea notifications use a different signal (breathing disturbances estimated from wrist movement), shown separately in this report when your export contains it.
findings.caveat: Apple Watch support in this report has so far been tested only on a generated export.

findings.title: Apple's breathing disturbances
findings.headline: Your Apple Watch estimates breathing disturbances from wrist movement during sleep; your typical night's value was {breathing_disturbances_median:.1f}. Apple's sleep apnea notification checks these values over 30 days and notifies you when they're elevated on at least half the nights; the Health app shows whether that happened.
findings.detail: Apple tuned the notification to avoid false alarms. In the FDA validation cohort it detected 66.3% of moderate-to-severe sleep apnea (sensitivity) and correctly stayed silent for 98.5% of people with normal or mild results (specificity); in Apple's own test set the figures were 66.6% and 95.9%. It needs at least 10 nights with a value in the 30-day window.
findings.caveat: About a third of moderate-to-severe cases go unnoticed, and the FDA clearance states the feature isn't intended to diagnose sleep apnea. This report doesn't know Apple's threshold for 'elevated', so it doesn't flag your values itself.
